content:
I have been going through the tutorial books in lean but I a stuck on the use cases of def. From what I understood:

  1. abbrev acts as the typical typedef in language where for abbrev A := B, A and B are definitionally and behaviorally identical
  2. structure (same with inductive) define a completely separate type with its own rules and behaviour
    I am mainly confused as to how def fits in the picture as one could do the following:
    def MyNat := Nat, where definitionally they are equal but I can define different rules for addition/OfNat etc. I think my confusion is at, if we want to prove statements for MyNat, wouldn't Lean treat it as Nat?

One thing that helped me at some point is to note that abbrev is transparent when Lean is trying to find type class instances, but def is not:

abbrev OtherNat := Nat
#check (5 : OtherNat) -- works

def MyNat := Nat
#check (5 : MyNat) -- does NOT work, no instance `OfNat MyNat 5`

The question of how abbrev differs is in transparency , see Transparency. The biggest difference is that def is not implicit_reducible/reducible by default, so abbrev is like a @[reducible] def ( see Abbrev which says as much).
I think my confusion mostly stemmed from the difference between definitional and semantical equalities, which the page Equality helped. Thank you for the responses!

abbrev acts as the typical typedef in language where for abbrev A := B, A and B are definitionally and behaviorally identical

This is "almost true" except when it is sometimes not (e.g. rw tactic doesn't see through it). The true "behaviorally identical" things are notation and custom syntax

As a rule of thumb, I would say that when defining a type alias you should probably go with either abbrev or structure.

Use abbrev when you want to just document slightly different use/meaning of the type and structure when you want to attach different operations to the type via type classes.

I'm not sure if there is actually sound use of deffor a type alias. For def MyNat := Nat Lean would sometimes treat MyNat as Nat(like Nat.succ a is valid for a : MyNat) and sometimes as a different type(type class synthesis, most tactics,...).

AFAIK the term "type alias" usually refers to defs which have different instances than the type they're actually defined as, so a type alias is never abbrev.

Tomas Skrivan said:

I'm not sure if there is actually sound use of deffor a type alias.

see #lean4 > linter for instance diamonds @ 💬

I'm not sure if this is the right way to interpret this but I experimented with the following snippet:

def MyNat := Nat

instance : Add  MyNat where
  add x y:= Nat.mul x y

def myNum : MyNat  := (38: Nat)
def myNum2 : MyNat := (3: Nat)
#eval Nat.add myNum  myNum2
-- Evaluates to : 41
#eval myNum  + myNum2
-- Evaluates to: 114

If I understood this right, any theorems/propositions that used the Nat type will work for the MyNat type due to a) The two being definitionally equal b) The proofs for Nat used operations such Nat.add which translate to the MyNat as well. If I override the MyNat Add, I basically define a new function MyNat.add which won't affect any theorems as those use the Nat.add function.

Christos Demetriou said:

If I understood this right, any theorems/propositions that used the Nat type will work for the MyNat

This depends on what you mean by "work". If you mean "use the apply tactic for a Nat theorem in a MyNat situation" then this will work, and if you mean "use the rw tactic for a Nat theorem in a MyNat situation" then this will not work. Some tactics/algorithms work up to syntactic equality, others up to definitional equality.
